words.definition: To praise someone or something highly and publicly.
words.example: Critics lauded the young pianist's debut, calling it the finest performance of the season.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'applaud' — clapping loudly to show admiration.

words.definition: To praise someone or something very highly and enthusiastically.
words.example: At the retirement dinner, colleagues rose one by one to extol her decades of quiet, tireless service.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'ex-toll' — you ring the bell (toll) again and again to loudly celebrate someone.

words.definition: To express formal, strong disapproval of someone's actions.
words.example: The senate voted to censure the official for misusing public funds.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'censor' — an official clamping down on wrongdoing.

words.definition: To speak about someone or something in a way that suggests little worth.
words.example: She never disparaged her rivals, even when they mocked her openly.
words.mnemonic: Starts with 'dis' — like dissing someone to lower their rank.

words.definition: To unfairly attack the good reputation of a person or thing.
words.example: The ad campaign tried to denigrate the competitor by hinting its products were unsafe.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'niger' (black) — to blacken someone's name.

words.definition: To mock or laugh at someone with contempt.
words.example: Colleagues derided his plan as hopeless until it doubled the company's profits.
words.mnemonic: 'De' + 'ride' — picture riding down on someone while laughing.

words.definition: To criticize someone very harshly and severely.
words.example: The judge excoriated the company for dumping chemicals into the river.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'ex-' + 'corium' (skin) — a verbal skinning-alive.

words.definition: To scold or attack someone with harsh words.
words.example: The manager lambasted the crew for leaving the site unlocked overnight.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'lamb basted' — but here someone gets a verbal basting.

words.definition: To say cruel and false things meant to make others hate someone.
words.example: The tabloids vilified the actress, painting her as a villain she never was.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'vil' as in 'villain' — to cast someone as the bad guy.

words.definition: To spread harmful and untrue statements about a person.
words.example: He felt maligned by rumors that he had cheated to win the contract.
words.mnemonic: 'Mal-' means bad (as in malignant) — to speak badly of someone.

words.definition: To scold or punish someone severely for wrongdoing.
words.example: The teacher chastised the students for copying answers during the test.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'chaste' — to discipline someone into proper behavior.

words.definition: To express disappointment with someone for a fault or failing.
words.example: She reproached him gently for forgetting their anniversary again.
words.mnemonic: 'Re' + 'proach' (approach) — approaching someone to point out a fault.

words.definition: To sharply criticize someone for something they have done.
words.example: The referee rebuked the player for arguing and showed him a yellow card.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 're-buck' — bucking someone back for misbehaving.

words.definition: To tell someone, usually gently, that they have done wrong.
words.example: The librarian reproved the children for whispering, then smiled and let them stay.
words.mnemonic: 'Re' + 'prove' — proving someone at fault so they correct it.

words.definition: To warn or gently scold someone about a fault or danger.
words.example: The doctor admonished her to cut back on salt before her blood pressure worsened.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'monish' from Latin 'monere' (to warn) — same root as 'monitor.'

words.definition: To scold someone sharply for a fault or wrongdoing.
words.example: The coach upbraided the players for showing up late to practice yet again.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'up-braid' — picture someone yanking your braid UP while angrily telling you off.

words.definition: To criticize someone angrily and at great length.
words.example: She berated the waiter so loudly that the whole restaurant fell silent.
words.mnemonic: BE + RATE — imagine a furious boss who 'be-rates' your work at zero while shouting.

words.definition: To punish or reprimand someone very severely.
words.example: The judge castigated the company for ignoring safety warnings for years.
words.mnemonic: 'Cast-a-gate' — hear the heavy cast-iron GATE slamming shut on the guilty as punishment.

words.definition: Severely and bitterly critical in a way meant to wound.
words.example: The critic's scathing review shut the play down after a single night.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'scalding' — the words burn you like scalding-hot water.

words.definition: So excessive as to seem insincere or distasteful, especially in flattery.
words.example: His fulsome compliments about the boss's brilliance made everyone in the room cringe.
words.mnemonic: Read it as 'FULL-some' — so FULL of flattery it becomes sickening.

words.definition: A public speech or piece of writing that formally expresses high praise.
words.example: At the retirement dinner she delivered a panegyric honoring forty years of service.
words.mnemonic: PANE-gyric — picture a stained-glass PANE dedicated to a hero, glowing with glory.

words.definition: A formal tribute expressing warm, enthusiastic approval.
words.example: The professor's encomium to her late mentor moved the whole audience to tears.
words.mnemonic: En-COME-i-um — everyone COMEs together to sing your praises.

words.definition: To speak or write in high praise of someone, often after their death.
words.example: The senator was asked to eulogize his old friend at the memorial service.
words.mnemonic: EU (Greek for 'good') + LOG — you LOG all the GOOD things about a person.

words.definition: To regard someone or something with the deepest respect, often as sacred.
words.example: Pilgrims travel for weeks to venerate the relics housed in the ancient cathedral.
words.mnemonic: Kin to 'venerable' — a VENERABLE white-haired elder you treat with awe.

words.definition: To feel profound respect and admiration for someone.
words.example: Students still revere the teacher who first made them fall in love with reading.
words.mnemonic: Think 'reverend' — a figure you look up to with quiet awe.

words.definition: To respect and admire someone or something greatly.
words.example: Her colleagues esteemed her not only for her skill but for her fairness.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'a team' — a strong TEAM holds every member in high regard.

words.definition: To praise someone formally or officially.
words.example: The mayor commended the firefighters for their bravery during the rescue.
words.mnemonic: Hidden 'MEND' — you praise the person who helped MEND the problem.

words.definition: Enthusiastic public approval or applause.
words.example: Her debut novel won such acclaim that it sold out within a week.
words.mnemonic: AC + CLAIM — a cheering crowd loudly CLAIMs you're the best.

words.definition: An enthusiastic expression of approval or applause.
words.example: The young pianist earned plaudits from even the sternest judges on the panel.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with 'applaud' — plaudits are the applause you collect.

words.definition: An award or mark of honor recognizing an achievement.
words.example: Winning the Nobel Prize was the crowning accolade of her long career.
words.mnemonic: From the knighting ceremony — picture the flat of a blade tapping your shoulder to honor you.

words.definition: To praise someone too much or insincerely, usually to win their favor.
words.example: He tried to flatter the manager by calling her the smartest person in the building.
words.mnemonic: FLAT + BUTTER: you 'butter someone up', spreading praise on smooth and thick.

words.definition: To give someone exaggerated attention and affection to gain their approval.
words.example: The waiters fawned over the celebrity, refilling her glass before it was ever empty.
words.mnemonic: Picture a baby deer (a fawn) nuzzling and trailing anyone who feeds it, eager for approval.

words.definition: Overly eager to please or obey in a servile, insincere way.
words.example: The obsequious clerk bowed twice and agreed with every word the customer said.
words.mnemonic: Say it 'ob-SEEK-we-us': they SEEK to please US at every turn.

words.definition: A person who flatters powerful people to gain advantage for themselves.
words.example: The king was surrounded by sycophants who cheered his every whim.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'sick elephant' — a sick elephant lumbering after the boss, nodding at everything.

words.definition: Excessive admiration or praise directed at someone.
words.example: The young star basked in the adulation of thousands of screaming fans.
words.mnemonic: ADORE + elATION: adoration cranked all the way up to worshipful elation.

words.definition: Formal or official approval and commendation.
words.example: The committee's approbation meant her research would finally receive funding.
words.mnemonic: Hear APPROVE hiding inside it: approbation = APPROVE-ation (Latin 'approbare', to approve).

words.definition: Harsh public criticism and the shame that comes with it.
words.example: The senator faced widespread opprobrium after the bribery scandal broke.
words.mnemonic: Op-PROBE-rium: the press PROBES your wrongdoing and buries you in disgrace.

words.definition: A false statement made deliberately to damage someone's reputation.
words.example: The calumny that he stole from the charity was later proven a complete fabrication.
words.mnemonic: CALL-um-ny: a poisonous 'call' of lies shouted against your good name.

words.definition: To make false spoken statements that harm someone's reputation.
words.example: She threatened to sue the broadcaster who slandered her on the live show.
words.mnemonic: SLUR + under: a spoken slur that drags a person's name UNDER.

words.definition: To harm someone's good reputation by spreading false information.
words.example: The tabloid was sued for trying to defame the actor with invented affairs.
words.mnemonic: de- (remove) + FAME: to strip away someone's good name and fame.

words.definition: To publicly attack, mock, or expose someone to ridicule.
words.example: Critics pilloried the mayor in every newspaper after the budget collapsed.
words.mnemonic: A pillory was the wooden frame that locked people in the town square to be jeered at — so to pillory is to put someone up for public shaming.

words.definition: To publicly condemn something as wrong or bad.
words.example: Activists gathered to decry the new law as an attack on free speech.
words.mnemonic: de- (down) + CRY: to 'cry down' loudly against something.

words.definition: To make someone or something seem unimportant or of low value.
words.example: He belittled her achievements, calling her promotion nothing more than luck.
words.mnemonic: be + LITTLE: to make a person feel tiny and insignificant.

words.definition: To express strong disapproval of something.
words.example: The professor deprecated the habit of memorizing facts without understanding them.
words.mnemonic: de-PRECIOUS-ate: to treat something as NOT precious, i.e., to run it down.

words.definition: To complain or find fault continually over small matters.
words.example: Instead of helping, he just carped about how the dishes were stacked wrong.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'harp' — someone who carps keeps harping on the same petty gripes.

words.definition: To raise trivial complaints or find fault over unimportant details.
words.example: Instead of praising the plan, he would cavil about the exact wording of every footnote.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'cavity' — a tiny hole you keep poking at, just as a caviler keeps poking at tiny faults.

words.definition: A long, forceful, and often scolding speech aimed at an audience.
words.example: The coach launched into a twenty-minute harangue about our lazy defense until everyone stared at the floor.
words.mnemonic: Har-ANG — picture an ANGry speaker ranting on and on without pause.

words.definition: A bitter, abusive speech or piece of writing that attacks someone or something.
words.example: Her restaurant review swelled into a diatribe against the entire fast-food industry.
words.mnemonic: Say 'die-a-tribe' — an attack fierce enough to take down a whole tribe.

words.definition: Harsh, abusive language used to attack or condemn someone.
words.example: The town-hall debate collapsed into personal invective the moment tempers flared.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'infective' — words so venomous they seem to infect the air.

words.definition: To attack or criticize someone with harsh, bitter words.
words.example: Angry citizens vituperated the mayor for hours after the water supply was cut.
words.mnemonic: Hidden inside is 'viper' — a viper's venomous 'berate' is to vituperate.

words.definition: To scold or express mild disapproval toward someone.
words.example: She gently chided the puppy for chewing yet another slipper.
words.mnemonic: 'Chide' contains 'chi(l)d' — you chide a child for small misbehavior.

words.definition: Expressing warm approval or high praise.
words.example: The debut film earned laudatory notices from every major critic in the country.
words.mnemonic: 'Laud' echoes 'applaud' — laudatory words applaud whatever they describe.

words.definition: Deserving reward, honor, or praise because of worthy qualities.
words.example: The firefighter received a medal for meritorious service during the warehouse rescue.
words.mnemonic: MERIT-orious — so full of merit that it earns honor.

words.definition: Serving as an outstanding model that others should follow.
words.example: Her exemplary attendance record made her the obvious choice for the leadership award.
words.mnemonic: EXEMPLARY holds 'example' — an example so good it sets the standard.

words.definition: Deserving of respect and high regard.
words.example: The estimable judge was known throughout the state for her unshakable fairness.
words.mnemonic: You hold an estimable person in high 'esteem' — same root.

words.definition: Deserving approval and admiration for being good or well done.
words.example: Giving up every weekend to tutor kids is a genuinely praiseworthy commitment.
words.mnemonic: Break it in two: 'praise' + 'worthy' — literally worth being praised.

words.definition: Mockery or ridicule directed at something treated as ridiculous.
words.example: His theory that the moon is hollow was met with hoots of derision from the panel.
words.mnemonic: Contains Latin 'risi' (to laugh) — cruel laughter aimed at someone.

words.definition: A feeling that someone or something is worthless and beneath consideration.
words.example: She looked at the student who had cheated with open contempt.
words.mnemonic: Con-TEMPT — someone so low they 'can't tempt' you into any respect.

words.definition: A feeling that someone or something is unworthy of one's attention or respect.
words.example: He tossed the cheap plastic trophy aside with obvious disdain.
words.mnemonic: DIS-dain — to 'dis' someone, treating them as beneath you.

words.definition: Open dislike and lack of respect, often mixed with mockery.
words.example: The veteran actor poured scorn on the newcomer's clumsy, over-rehearsed performance.
words.mnemonic: SCORN sounds like 'scorch' — you scorch someone with your withering disrespect.

words.definition: To make fun of a person or thing in a cruel, contemptuous way.
words.example: The other kids ridiculed his homemade costume until he left the party in tears.
words.mnemonic: RIDICULE sounds like 'ridiculous' — you make someone seem ridiculous.

words.definition: To imitate or laugh at someone scornfully in order to belittle them.
words.example: He mocked her accent by exaggerating every word she spoke.
words.mnemonic: A 'mock' exam fakes the real thing; mocking fakes and imitates to insult.

words.definition: To provoke someone with insulting or teasing remarks.
words.example: The rival fans taunted the goalkeeper every time he touched the ball.
words.mnemonic: TAUNT sounds like 'haunt' — a taunt haunts you with nagging insults.

words.definition: To shout rude, mocking remarks at someone.
words.example: The crowd jeered as the referee made yet another terrible call.
words.mnemonic: JEER rhymes with 'sneer' and 'leer' — all hostile faces and sounds.

words.definition: An insulting or sarcastic remark meant to provoke.
words.example: She ignored his gibe about her cooking and calmly served dessert.
words.mnemonic: GIBE sounds like 'jab' — a verbal jab that pokes at you.

words.definition: To smile or speak in a scornful way that shows contempt.
words.example: He sneered at the cheap wine, refusing to take even a single sip.
words.mnemonic: The 'sn-' curls your nose and lip in scorn, like a snarl.

words.definition: To reduce the value, worth, or good impression of something.
words.example: The loud wallpaper detracted from the otherwise elegant room.
words.mnemonic: DE- (away) + TRACT (pull) — to pull away from something's value.

words.definition: To make or become smaller, weaker, or less important.
words.example: The medicine slowly diminished her pain over the course of a few hours.
words.mnemonic: DIMINISH contains 'mini' — to make something mini, or smaller.

words.definition: To express strong disapproval of something, often publicly.
words.example: World leaders condemned the attack on unarmed civilians.
words.mnemonic: CONDEMN ends in 'demn' like 'damn' — to damn someone's actions.

words.definition: To publicly declare that someone or something is wrong or evil.
words.example: The senator denounced the policy as cruel and deeply unjust.
words.mnemonic: DE- + NOUNCE (announce) — to announce against someone openly.

words.definition: To scold someone formally for a fault or wrongdoing.
words.example: The officer was reprimanded for leaving his post early.
words.mnemonic: A reprimand from your 'command'er is an official telling-off.

words.definition: An expression of blame or criticism for a fault.
words.example: A stern reproof from the teacher silenced the whispering students.
words.mnemonic: 'Proof' that you did wrong, handed back to you as blame.

words.definition: Strong public criticism or abusive language that harms a reputation.
words.example: After the scandal, the once-admired mayor faced years of obloquy.
words.mnemonic: OB- (against) + LOQU (speak, as in loquacious) — speaking against someone.

words.definition: A false or damaging remark that attacks someone's character.
words.example: He sued the newspaper for casting aspersions on his honesty.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'a-spersion' from dispersion — spraying dirt on a reputation.

words.definition: Sharp, clear, and forceful in expression or thought.
words.example: Her trenchant analysis exposed every flaw in the proposal.
words.mnemonic: Like a 'trench' cut sharply into the ground — cutting, incisive words.

words.definition: Making false and insulting claims meant to damage someone's reputation.
words.example: The tabloid printed scurrilous rumors that the senator had embezzled charity funds.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'scurry' + 'lie' — nasty lies that scurry around town damaging names.

words.definition: Ordinary and dull, lacking imagination or excitement.
words.example: She had hoped for an exotic honeymoon, but they settled for a prosaic weekend at a roadside motel.
words.mnemonic: 'Prose' + '-aic' — plain everyday prose, not soaring poetry.

words.definition: Expressing much in very few words; briefly and bluntly spoken.
words.example: When asked how the battle went, the general gave a laconic 'We won.'
words.mnemonic: From Laconia (Sparta), whose warriors were famous for terse, blunt replies.

words.definition: Using far more words than necessary; long-winded.
words.example: His verbose report ran forty pages when a single paragraph would have done.
words.mnemonic: 'Verb' + '-ose' — overflowing with words, like 'grandiose' excess.

words.definition: Talking too much, especially about unimportant things.
words.example: The garrulous barber chattered nonstop about his neighbors while cutting my hair.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'gargle' — someone endlessly gargling out words, bubbling on and on.

words.definition: Habitually saying little; reserved and uncommunicative.
words.example: Her taciturn grandfather would sit through entire dinners without offering a single remark.
words.mnemonic: 'Tacit' (silent, unspoken) + 'turn' — a person who turns silent.

words.definition: Tending to talk a great deal; very chatty.
words.example: The loquacious tour guide barely paused for breath during the three-hour walk.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'loqui' = to speak (as in eloquent, soliloquy) — full of speech.

words.definition: Overly concerned with minor details or rules, and showing off learning.
words.example: The pedantic professor deducted points for a misplaced comma in an otherwise brilliant essay.
words.mnemonic: From 'pedagogue' (teacher) — picture a nitpicky teacher fixated on tiny rules.

words.definition: Having or showing deep, wide-ranging knowledge gained through study.
words.example: The erudite historian could quote medieval texts from memory in three languages.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'e-RUDE-ite' but is the opposite: Latin 'erudire' drags you out of rawness into learning.

words.definition: Showing keen judgment and deep practical wisdom.
words.example: The sagacious old lawyer foresaw the trap in the contract that everyone else missed.
words.mnemonic: 'Sage' (a wise person) + '-acious' — full of sage wisdom.

words.definition: Quick to grasp situations and act to one's advantage; shrewd.
words.example: One astute investor sold her shares the week before the company collapsed.
words.mnemonic: 'A-stute' sounds like 'a student' who's razor-sharp and never fooled.

words.definition: Having a keen ability to notice and understand what is not obvious.
words.example: The perspicacious detective noticed the faint tan line where a wedding ring had been.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'spec/spic' (to see, as in spectacles) — sees clearly through anything.

words.definition: Honest, open expression free from evasion or flattery.
words.example: With surprising candor, the CEO admitted the product launch had been a disaster.
words.mnemonic: Think 'candle' — it throws light on everything and hides nothing.

words.definition: To speak vaguely or ambiguously in order to mislead or avoid commitment.
words.example: When reporters pressed him on the budget, the mayor equivocated instead of giving a straight answer.
words.mnemonic: 'Equi-' (equal) + 'voc' (voice) — giving two meanings equal weight so no one can pin you down.

words.definition: To deliberately make something confusing or hard to understand.
words.example: The company used dense legal jargon to obfuscate the fees buried in the contract.
words.mnemonic: 'Ob-FOG-cate' — to throw fog over something (Latin 'fuscare', to darken) so it can't be seen.
